noteBlocks.lede: Ask only about the pupils who take under 26 minutes to walk to school, and the whole picture shrinks to them. "Given that" does exactly this: it makes a smaller world and asks a probability inside it. On a normal curve, or in a binomial count, that smaller world is usually one region sitting inside another.
can: Find a conditional probability from two tails of a normal curve
Find one from two binomial probabilities, given at least one success
Spot a nested pair of events and divide, never multiply

noteBlocks.alt: A normal curve of walking times with mean 20 minutes. The region under 26 minutes is shaded lightly; the region under 15 minutes is shaded darker and sits inside it.
noteBlocks.caption: Walking times to school. The light region is everyone under 26 minutes; the dark region inside it is everyone under 15.

noteBlocks.md:
Walking times to school are normally distributed with mean 20 minutes and standard deviation 4. For a pupil picked at random, the chance she takes under 15 minutes is the dark tail, 0.1056.
Now add a condition: **given that** she takes under 26 minutes. Every pupil beyond 26 minutes is set aside, and the light region left is the new whole.
The question is now asked inside the light region. The dark region is the part of it that is also under 15 minutes, so the answer is dark as a share of light: the dark area divided by the light area.

noteBlocks.prompt: On the walking-time curve, a pupil is known to take under 26 minutes. Which region is now the whole, the one everything is measured against?
options: The light region: everyone under 26 minutes
The dark region: everyone under 15 minutes
The whole curve: every pupil
noteBlocks.answer: The light region: everyone under 26 minutes
noteBlocks.explain: "Given that she takes under 26 minutes" sets aside every pupil beyond 26, so on the curve only the light region is left, and it becomes the whole. The dark region is the part of it you are asked about. So the whole is the light region, and the answer to such a question is dark over light.

noteBlocks.md:
Look again at where the dark region sits: entirely inside the light one. Every pupil under 15 minutes is automatically under 26. Two events like these are **nested**: the smaller event lies inside the larger.
That keeps the calculation short. "Under 15 and under 26" is not a new event to build; it is simply "under 15".

noteBlocks.title: Conditional Probability
noteBlocks.why: The same 'given that' idea on a two-way table: the group named after 'given' becomes the whole, and the answer is a share of it. Watch the bottom of each fraction change; the curve does exactly the same.

noteBlocks.md:
The same idea with counts. Suppose 80 of 100 pupils take under 26 minutes, and 12 of those take under 15.
Given under 26 minutes, the whole is those 80. The 12 sit inside them, so the probability is their share: $\frac{12}{80} = 0.15$.

noteBlocks.prompt: In another school, 75 pupils take under 26 minutes to walk in, and 18 of those take under 15. Given that a pupil takes under 26 minutes, what is the probability that she takes under 15?
noteBlocks.explain: The condition names the whole: the 75 pupils under 26 minutes, just as the 80 were the whole a moment ago. The 18 under 15 minutes sit inside them, so the answer is their share of the whole: 18 ÷ 75, which is 0.24.

noteBlocks.alt: A probability line from 0 to 1. P(A) is marked at 0.35 and P(A given B) further to the right at 0.5, with an arrow showing the move.
noteBlocks.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 400 134' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='A probability line from 0 to 1 with P(A) at 0.35 and P(A given B) further right at 0.5'><title>A probability line from 0 to 1 with P(A) at 0.35 and P(A given B) further right at 0.5</title><path d='M 30 74 L 370 74' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.6' fill='none' stroke-linejoin='round' stroke-linecap='round'/><path d='M 30 66 L 30 82' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.4' fill='none' stroke-linejoin='round' stroke-linecap='round'/><path d='M 370 66 L 370 82' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.4' fill='none' stroke-linejoin='round' stroke-linecap='round'/><circle cx='149' cy='74' r='6' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.35'/><circle cx='200' cy='74' r='6' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.9'/><path d='M 157 56 L 192 56 M 185 51 L 192 56 L 185 61' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.3' fill='none' stroke-linejoin='round' stroke-linecap='round'/><g font-family='inherit' font-size='15' fill='currentColor' text-anchor='middle'><text x='30' y='102' font-weight='600'>0</text><text x='370' y='102' font-weight='600'>1</text><text x='149' y='34'>P(A) = 0.35</text><text x='200' y='126' font-weight='600'>P(A | B) = 0.5</text><text x='370' y='126' text-anchor='end' font-size='14'>never past 1</text></g></svg>
noteBlocks.caption: Dividing by a probability below 1 pushes the value to the right. It grows, and it can never pass 1.

noteBlocks.md:
For a nested pair, the conditional probability is always at least as big as the plain one, because you divide by a probability less than 1. On the line, $P(A) = 0.35$ inside a group of probability $0.7$ becomes $\frac{0.35}{0.7} = 0.5$.
It can never be more than 1: the smaller region cannot be bigger than the region it sits inside.

So hold every answer against both limits. For the walking times, $0.1056 \div 0.9332 = 0.1132$: a little bigger than 0.1056, and well under 1. Divide the other way round and you get 8.84, which cannot be a probability. An answer above 1 means the fraction is upside down.

noteBlocks.prompt: A pupil works out a conditional probability for a nested pair of events and gets 2.5. What has happened?
options: The fraction is upside down: the larger probability was divided by the smaller
Nothing: a conditional probability can be more than 1
The two probabilities should have been multiplied instead
noteBlocks.answer: The fraction is upside down: the larger probability was divided by the smaller
noteBlocks.explain: On the probability line, a nested conditional sits between the plain probability and 1, never beyond 1. Dividing the larger probability by the smaller always gives more than 1, which is how 2.5 appears. So the fraction is upside down: turn it over, small over large, and divide again.

noteBlocks.text: Why the top is the small region alone

noteBlocks.title: On the formula sheet
noteBlocks.md: $P(A \mid B) = \dfrac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)}$: $A$ given $B$ is $A$ and $B$ together, over $B$ (FM3-PRB-02; the Unit 3 formula sheet).

The sheet puts $P(A \cap B)$, both events at once, on top. When $A$ sits inside $B$, every outcome in $A$ is already in $B$, so "both" is exactly $A$.
For the walking times ($A$ under 15, $B$ under 26): $P(A \cap B) = P(A)$, which is 0.1056, over $P(B) = 0.9332$. Nothing is multiplied.

noteBlocks.title: Why multiplying fails here
noteBlocks.md: Multiplying gives "both" only for independent events, which leave each other alone. Being under 15 minutes settles being under 26 completely, so these two are as far from independent as events can be.

noteBlocks.prompt: Bus journeys: $A$ is "under 29 minutes" and $B$ is "under 41.6 minutes". What is $P(A \cap B)$?
options: $P(A)$, because every journey under 29 minutes is also under 41.6
$P(A) \times P(B)$, because "and" means multiply
$P(B)$, because it is the larger event
noteBlocks.answer: $P(A)$, because every journey under 29 minutes is also under 41.6
noteBlocks.explain: Picture the two regions on a curve: under 29 minutes sits inside under 41.6, exactly as under 15 sat inside under 26. So "both" adds nothing and is the small region itself. A product would be right only for independent events, and these two decide each other. So $P(A \cap B) = P(A)$.

noteBlocks.alt: A normal curve of bus journey times with mean 35 minutes. The region under 41.6 minutes is shaded lightly and the region under 29 minutes is shaded darker inside it.
noteBlocks.caption: Bus journeys with mean 35 minutes and standard deviation 6. Under 29 sits inside under 41.6: dark over light.

noteBlocks.md:
Bus journeys have mean 35 minutes and standard deviation 6. Given that a journey takes under 41.6 minutes, find the probability that it takes under 29.
**Step 1.** The condition: $z = \frac{41.6 - 35}{6}$, so $z = 1.1$, and the table gives $P(T < 41.6) = 0.8643$.

**Step 2.** The inner event: $z = \frac{29 - 35}{6}$, so $z = -1$. A left tail below a negative $z$ is folded: $1 - 0.8413 = 0.1587$.
**Step 3.** Small over large: $\frac{0.1587}{0.8643} = 0.1836$, to 4 decimal places. It is bigger than 0.1587 and below 1, as it must be.

noteBlocks.prompt: Queueing times at a canteen have mean 12 minutes and standard deviation 2.5. From the table, $P(T < 15) = 0.8849$ and $P(T < 8.5) = 0.0808$. Work out $P(T < 8.5 \mid T < 15)$ to 4 decimal places.
noteBlocks.explain: As with the bus journeys, under 8.5 minutes sits inside under 15, so the top is the small tail alone and the bottom is the condition's tail: $\frac{0.0808}{0.8849}$, which is 0.0913. Multiplying on top would hand back 0.0808; dividing the other way would give more than 1.

noteBlocks.alt: A normal curve of plank lengths with mean 240 cm. The region over 236 cm is shaded lightly and the region over 246 cm is shaded darker inside it.
noteBlocks.caption: Plank lengths with mean 240 cm and standard deviation 4 cm. Over 246 sits inside over 236: the far tail inside the near one.

noteBlocks.md:
When both events say "more than", the picture flips to the right. Planks have mean 240 cm and standard deviation 4 cm. Given that a plank is over 236 cm, find the probability that it is over 246 cm.
Over 246 is the far right tail, and it lies inside over 236. Dark over light again.

**Step 1.** The condition: $z = \frac{236 - 240}{4}$, so $z = -1$. Everything to the right of a negative $z$ is the table value itself: $P(L > 236) = 0.8413$.
**Step 2.** $z = \frac{246 - 240}{4}$, so $z = 1.5$, and a right tail is $1 - 0.9332 = 0.0668$.
**Step 3.** $\frac{0.0668}{0.8413} = 0.0794$.

noteBlocks.prompt: Parcels at a depot have mean mass 12 kg and standard deviation 1.5 kg. From the table, $P(M > 11.1) = 0.7257$ and $P(M > 14.7) = 0.0359$. Work out $P(M > 14.7 \mid M > 11.1)$ to 4 decimal places.
noteBlocks.explain: Over 14.7 kg is the far right tail, and like the planks over 246 cm it sits inside the condition, over 11.1 kg. So the far tail goes on top and the near one on the bottom: $\frac{0.0359}{0.7257}$, which is 0.0495.

noteBlocks.caption: Four scratch cards. Every count in 'at least 2' also sits in 'at least 1', so the two events are nested.

noteBlocks.md:
Four scratch cards each win with probability 0.4, independently. Given that at least one wins, find the probability that at least two win.
The dots show why this is the same idea: every count in "at least 2" is also in "at least 1". Both probabilities come from the complement, 1 minus the counts left out.

noteBlocks.prompt: Five seeds each germinate with probability 0.3, independently, so $P(X \geq 1) = 0.83193$ and $P(X \geq 2) = 0.47178$. Given that at least one germinates, what is the probability that at least two do? Give 4 decimal places.
noteBlocks.explain: As with the scratch cards, at least 2 sits inside at least 1, so the smaller probability goes on top: $\frac{0.47178}{0.83193}$, which is 0.5671. The bottom is "at least one", $1 - P(0)$, never $P(1)$ on its own.

noteBlocks.caption: Six coin tosses. 'Exactly 3 heads' is a single count, and it sits inside 'at least 1 head'.

noteBlocks.md:
A fair coin is tossed six times. Given at least one head, find the probability of exactly three.
Exactly three is one count, and it lies inside at least one. So the top is a single term of the expansion, and the bottom is 1 minus the no-heads term.

**Step 1.** $P(3) = 20 \times 0.5^{3} \times 0.5^{3}$, which is $0.3125$, with 20 from row 6 of Pascal's triangle.
**Step 2.** $P(X \geq 1) = 1 - 0.5^{6}$, which is $0.984375$.
**Step 3.** $\frac{0.3125}{0.984375} = 0.3175$. A little bigger than 0.3125, as a nested conditional must be.

noteBlocks.prompt: Five seeds each germinate with probability 0.3, independently, so $P(X = 2) = 0.3087$ and $P(X \geq 1) = 0.83193$. Given that at least one germinates, what is the probability that exactly two do? Give 4 decimal places.
noteBlocks.explain: Exactly two is one count inside at least one, just as exactly three heads sat inside at least one head. So the single term goes on top and "at least one" on the bottom: $\frac{0.3087}{0.83193}$, which is 0.3711.

noteBlocks.text: See it done: the paper's shape

noteBlocks.alt: A normal curve of 400 m times with mean 85 seconds. The region under 95 seconds is shaded lightly and the region under 71 seconds is shaded darker inside it.
noteBlocks.caption: Times for 400 m with mean 85 seconds and standard deviation 8. Under 71 sits inside under 95.

noteBlocks.md:
On the paper this comes as three parts, the last worth 2 marks. Times for 400 m have mean 85 seconds and standard deviation 8.
**(i)** $z = \frac{95 - 85}{8}$, so $z = 1.25$ and $P(T < 95) = 0.8944$.
**(ii)** $z = \frac{71 - 85}{8}$, so $z = -1.75$; fold: $1 - 0.9599 = 0.0401$.
**(iii)** The fraction is $\frac{0.0401}{0.8944}$, which is $0.0448$.

noteBlocks.title: Where part (iii) loses its marks
noteBlocks.md: Part (iii) has 2 marks: the fraction with (ii) over (i), then its value. In both years it has been set, most candidates multiplied the two tails on top, which hands back the smaller tail unchanged. The strongest wrote (ii) over (i) and divided.

noteBlocks.prompt: For the same 400 m times, $P(T < 95) = 0.8944$ and $P(T < 79) = 0.2266$. Work out $P(T < 79 \mid T < 95)$ to 4 decimal places.
noteBlocks.explain: Under 79 seconds sits inside under 95, exactly as part (ii) sat inside part (i) above. So the small tail goes over the large one: $\frac{0.2266}{0.8944}$, which is 0.2534. The first mark is for that fraction, the second for its value.

noteBlocks.md: **The last part reuses the first two.** In 2022 and 2023 the normal question closed with a 2-mark 'given that' on parts (i) and (ii): no new table work, just (ii) over (i).

**"Does not" names the region.** Turn the words into an inequality first, as a 2021 normal question and many Venn questions needed. "Does not last more than 30 hours" is the left tail, $T < 30$, never $T > 30$.

**Units that do not match.** In 2026 the mean was in minutes and the time in hours: convert first. With mean 250 minutes and standard deviation 20, 4.5 hours is $4.5 \times 60 = 270$ minutes, so $z = \frac{270 - 250}{20}$, which is $1$.

noteBlocks.prompt: Battery life is normally distributed. A question asks for a probability given that a battery does not last more than 30 hours. Which region is the condition?
options: $T < 30$: the left tail below 30 hours
$T > 30$: the right tail above 30 hours
$T < 30$ and $T > 30$ together: the whole curve
noteBlocks.explain: "Does not last more than 30 hours" rules out every battery above 30 hours, so what is left is the left tail below 30. Turn the words into that inequality first, $T < 30$, and shade it; that tail is the whole the answer is measured against.

noteBlocks.md: **A nested pair on a tree.** 2019 asked for three the same given the first two the same, and 2024 for both green given both the same colour. The smaller event sits inside the condition, so its branch total alone goes on top.

**The condition is not the first stage.** In 2025 it was the second set, in 2026 rain on either day. Add every branch that meets it for the bottom. First stage 0.6; second 0.5 after it, 0.2 after a miss. Given the second, the bottom is $0.6 \times 0.5 + 0.4 \times 0.2 = 0.38$, and 'first missed' is $\frac{0.08}{0.38} = 0.2105$.

noteBlocks.prompt: A tree question: given that it rained at some point over the weekend, find the probability that Sunday was dry. What goes on the bottom of the fraction?
options: The total of every branch on which it rained at least once
The probability of rain on Sunday alone
1, because the whole weekend is the sample
noteBlocks.answer: The total of every branch on which it rained at least once
noteBlocks.explain: The condition, rain at some point, is met on every branch with rain on at least one day, just as both 'second' branches made the 0.38 above. Add those branches for the bottom. The top is the one branch among them where Sunday was dry.

noteBlocks.md: **Working back from a given conditional.** In 2026 the conditional probability was given and a count was asked for. Put the unknown count over the condition's count and set it equal to the value: if 40 pupils play hockey and a hockey player is in the county squad with probability $\frac{3}{8}$, then $\frac{x}{40} = \frac{3}{8}$, so $x = 15$.

noteBlocks.prompt: A choir has 60 members. Given that a pupil is in the choir, the probability that she also plays an instrument is 0.35. How many choir members play an instrument?
noteBlocks.explain: The condition, being in the choir, is the whole: 60 pupils, just as the 40 hockey players were. The unknown count over that whole equals the given probability, $\frac{x}{60} = 0.35$, so $x = 0.35 \times 60$, which is 21.

noteBlocks.caption: Three mornings. 'Exactly one quick round' is a single count inside 'at least one', the same nesting as before.

noteBlocks.md: The Teacher Guidance tests conditionals through the binomial and/or the normal, so the two can meet in one question. A delivery round's time has mean 95 minutes and standard deviation 8. For 85 minutes, $z = -1.25$, so the fold gives $P(T < 85) = 0.1056$. Call it $p$: the chance that one morning's round is quick.

Over three mornings, $P(1) = 3 \times 0.1056 \times 0.8944^{2}$, which is $0.2534$, and $P(X \geq 1) = 1 - 0.8944^{3}$, which is $0.2845$.
Given at least one quick morning, the probability of exactly one is $\frac{0.2534}{0.2845}$, which is $0.8907$.

noteBlocks.prompt: A delivery round's time is normal with mean 95 minutes. Over three mornings, which number becomes the $p$ of the binomial for "a round under 85 minutes"?
options: $P(T < 85) = 0.1056$, the probability of one quick morning
$P(T < 105) = 0.8944$, the larger tail
The conditional probability from the earlier part
noteBlocks.answer: $P(T < 85) = 0.1056$, the probability of one quick morning
noteBlocks.explain: Each morning is one trial, and a success is a round under 85 minutes, so the trial's probability is that tail from the table, 0.1056. The three mornings then follow the binomial with $p = 0.1056$, and only the last step conditions on the count.

noteBlocks.title: Where this specification stops
noteBlocks.md: Every conditional CCEA sets through a distribution is nested. A pair such as 'over 80 given under 95' would need the area between two values, which the Teacher Guidance keeps out, as it keeps out finding a value from a given probability.

noteBlocks.md:
Start from the sheet, $P(A \mid B) = \dfrac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)}$, and read it with the counts. Out of 100 pupils, $P(B) = \frac{80}{100}$, and $P(A \cap B) = \frac{12}{100}$ because the 12 are inside the 80.
Divide, and the 100s cancel: $\frac{12}{80} = 0.15$, the share of the box. With $A$ inside $B$, $A \cap B$ is $A$, so $P(A \mid B) = \frac{P(A)}{P(B)}$.

noteBlocks.prompt: When $A$ lies inside $B$, which single change turns the sheet's formula into the nested rule?
options: Replace $P(A \cap B)$ by $P(A)$, because 'both' is just $A$
Replace $P(B)$ by 1, because $B$ is certain
Replace $P(A \cap B)$ by $P(A) \times P(B)$
noteBlocks.answer: Replace $P(A \cap B)$ by $P(A)$, because 'both' is just $A$
noteBlocks.explain: On the grid, every dark dot is inside the dashed box, so 'in both' is the same set of pupils as 'dark'. That is why the top of the sheet's formula becomes $P(A)$. The bottom stays the condition's probability, $P(B)$, never 1.

noteBlocks.md:
Shrink the whole to the condition's region: the answer is a share of it.
Spot a nested pair: the small probability alone goes on top; divide, never multiply.
Normal: both tails from the table, then small over large, to 4 decimal places.
Binomial: 'at least one' is 1 minus P(0); the top is one term or a complement.
Read the twist first; check the answer sits above the plain probability and below 1.

This is usually the closing 2-mark part of the normal question, as in 2022 and 2023, with both tails already found in parts (i) and (ii); a binomial version can arrive the same way. The first mark is the fraction, the smaller event's probability over the condition's; the last is its value to 4 decimal places. Stuck: sketch both regions, and if one sits inside the other, write small over large and divide.

workedExamples.stem:
The masses of bags of flour filled by a machine are normally distributed with mean 1500 g and standard deviation 20 g. A bag is picked at random.
Given that its mass is less than 1524 g, find the probability that its mass is less than 1470 g.
Give your answer to 4 decimal places.

steps.decision: Sketch first: shade less than 1524 lightly and less than 1470 darker. The darker region sits inside the lighter one, so "both" is just the inner event and its probability alone goes on top.

options: Every value less than 1470 is also less than 1524, so "both" is just the first event
The smaller number always goes on top of a fraction
Multiplying the two tails on top would give the same answer
whyMenu.explain: The sheet's formula puts "both" on top. Because the 1470 region lies inside the 1524 region, "both" is the inner event itself. Multiplying the tails would only be right for independent events, and would hand back the smaller tail.

steps.decision: The condition first. 1524 is above the mean, so the region to its left is more than half the curve: the table value itself.
The inner event: 1470 is below the mean, so its left tail is the mirror image of the right tail above +1.5: 1 minus the table value.
Divide, rounding only at the end. A quick check: 0.0755 is bigger than 0.0668 and below 1, as a nested conditional must be.

workedExamples.stem:
The lengths of cables cut by a machine are normally distributed with mean 50 m and standard deviation 2.5 m. A cable is picked at random.
Given that it is longer than 48 m, find the probability that it is longer than 54 m.
Give your answer to 4 decimal places.

steps.decision: Sketch first: shade more than 48 lightly and more than 54 darker. The darker region sits inside the lighter one, so "both" is just the inner event and its probability alone goes on top.
The condition first. 48 is below the mean, so everything above it is more than half the curve: by symmetry, the table value itself, with nothing taken from 1.

options: The region above a negative z is the mirror image of the region below +0.8
The table gives the area to the right, so no subtraction is needed
A negative z always means the probability is the table value
whyMenu.explain: Reflect the curve in the mean: the region above z = -0.8 becomes the region below z = 0.8, which is exactly what the table gives. The table always gives the area to the left of a positive z.

steps.decision: The inner event: 54 is above the mean, so the region beyond it is a right-hand tail: 1 minus the table value.
Divide, rounding only at the end. A quick check: 0.0695 is bigger than 0.0548 and below 1, as a nested conditional must be.

workedExamples.stem:
A netball player scores from each shot with probability 0.4, independently. She takes 6 shots.
Given that she scores at least once, find the probability that she scores at least twice.
Give your answer to 4 decimal places.

steps.decision: Every count in 'at least 2' is also in 'at least 1', so the two events are nested and the smaller one's probability alone goes on top.

options: Every count from 2 to 6 is also a count from 1 to 6
The larger probability always goes on the bottom of any fraction
At least 2 and at least 1 are independent
whyMenu.explain: Nested means one set of outcomes lies inside the other: 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 are all among 1 to 6. So 'at least 2 and at least 1' is simply 'at least 2', and nothing is multiplied.

steps.decision: None means every shot misses, so it is q multiplied by itself six times.
Exactly one: the coefficient 6 from row 6 of Pascal's triangle, the one success and the 5 misses.
At least one leaves out only the count 0.
At least two is at least one with the count 1 taken off.
Divide and round once, at the end. Check: 0.8042 is bigger than 0.76672 and below 1.

workedExamples.stem:
A basketball player scores each free throw with probability 0.3, independently. She takes 6 free throws.
Given that she scores at least once, find the probability that she scores exactly twice.

steps.decision: Exactly two is one of the counts in 'at least one', so the single term goes on top and the condition on the bottom.

options: The count 2 is one of the counts 1 to 6
Exactly two and at least one cannot happen together
The bottom should be P(X = 1)
whyMenu.explain: If she scores exactly twice she has certainly scored at least once, so 'both' is just 'exactly two'. The bottom is every count from 1 upwards, 1 minus P(0), never P(1) on its own.

steps.decision: The coefficient 15 is from row 6 of Pascal's triangle; the power of p is the number of scores, the power of q the misses.
At least once is everything except scoring none.
Divide and round once. Check: 0.3674 is a little bigger than 0.324135, and below 1.

items.stem: Before the lesson, a check on earlier work. The probability of no heads in four tosses of a fair coin is 0.0625. What is the probability of at least one head?
items.skill: The complement of 'none' (from the binomial topic)

options.feedback: Yes: at least one head is everything except no heads, so it is $1 - 0.0625$. The same move gives the bottom of most binomial conditionals in this topic.
That is the probability of no heads at all. At least one head is everything else: $1 - 0.0625 = 0.9375$.
That is $4 \times 0.0625$. At least one head is simpler: everything except no heads, $1 - 0.0625 = 0.9375$.

items.stem: Another check on earlier work. The Normal Probability Table gives $\Phi(1.2) = 0.8849$. What is $P(Z < -1.2)$?
items.skill: A left tail below a negative z (from the normal-table topic)

options.feedback: Yes: the tail below $-1.2$ is the mirror image of the tail above $+1.2$, so it is $1 - 0.8849$.
That is the area to the left of $+1.2$, more than half the curve. The tail below $-1.2$ is small: $1 - 0.8849 = 0.1151$.
A probability is never negative. The tail below $-1.2$ is the mirror image of the tail above $+1.2$: $1 - 0.8849 = 0.1151$.

items.stem: One more from earlier work. Of 40 pupils, 25 walk to school, and 10 of the walkers live within a mile. A walker is picked at random. What is the probability that she lives within a mile?
items.skill: A conditional probability from counts (from the conditional probability topic)

options.feedback: Yes: 'a walker is picked' makes the 25 walkers the whole, and 10 of them live within a mile.
That divides by every pupil. The pupil picked is a walker, so the whole is the 25 walkers: $\frac{10}{25}$.
That is the probability of being a walker. The question asks, among walkers, for those within a mile: $\frac{10}{25}$.

items.stem: $T$ is normally distributed. What is the probability that both $T < 30$ and $T < 45$ hold?
items.skill: Recognising that 'both' is the inner event of a nested pair

options.feedback: Yes: every value under 30 is also under 45, so 'both' is just $T < 30$.
A product is 'both' only for independent events. Here being under 30 settles being under 45, so 'both' is just $P(T < 30)$.
That is the larger event. 'Both' needs a value under 30 as well, and every such value is already under 45: $P(T < 30)$.

items.stem: Heights $H$ are normally distributed. Which expression gives $P(H > 180 \mid H > 170)$?
items.skill: Setting up the fraction for two 'more than' events

options.feedback: Yes: over 180 is the far tail, inside over 170, so it goes on top alone.
That is upside down and comes out above 1. The condition, over 170, goes on the bottom.
The product on top cancels and hands back $P(H > 180)$. Over 180 is inside over 170, so the top is $P(H > 180)$ alone.

items.stem: In a binomial question, which probability goes on the bottom of $P(X = 2 \mid X \geq 1)$?
items.skill: The condition 'at least one' as 1 minus P(0)

options.feedback: Yes: at least one is every count except 0.
That is exactly one. At least one also counts 2, 3 and upwards: $1 - P(0)$.
That is at least two: it leaves out the count 1, which 'at least one' includes. The bottom is $1 - P(0)$.

items.stem: Event $A$ lies inside event $B$, with $P(A) = 0.2$ and $P(B) = 0.5$. What is $P(A \mid B)$?
items.skill: The nested rule and the size check

options.feedback: Yes: $\frac{0.2}{0.5} = 0.4$, bigger than 0.2 and below 1, as a nested conditional must be.
That is $0.2 \times 0.5$, which would be 'both' for independent events. A conditional divides: $\frac{0.2}{0.5} = 0.4$.
Above 1, so the fraction is upside down. The condition goes on the bottom: $\frac{0.2}{0.5} = 0.4$.
That is $P(A)$ itself, as if the condition changed nothing. Given $B$, the whole shrinks to $B$: $\frac{0.2}{0.5} = 0.4$.

items.stem: In a binomial question, which fraction gives $P(X = 3 \mid X \geq 2)$?
items.skill: A condition other than 'at least one'

options.feedback: Yes: at least two leaves out the counts 0 and 1, and the count 3 sits inside it.
That bottom is at least one. The condition is at least two, so the count 1 must come off as well.
That reads 'at least two' as 'exactly two'. At least two is every count from 2 upwards: $1 - P(0) - P(1)$.

findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 5 gives the top of the fraction as the answer. He found both pieces, P(at least 2) and P(at least 1), but never divided one by the other. Given at least one win, the answer is a share of that condition: 0.4233 ÷ 0.7903.

prompts.prompt: Event A lies inside event B. What is P(A | B)?
prompts.answer: P(A) divided by P(B): because A is inside B, 'A and B' is just A.

prompts.prompt: Why must P(T < 34) not be multiplied by P(T < 60) on the top of the fraction?
prompts.answer: Multiplying gives 'both' only for independent events. Under 34 lies inside under 60, so 'both' is just P(T < 34).

prompts.prompt: What is the quick size check on a nested conditional probability?
prompts.answer: It is at least the smaller event's own probability and never above 1; above 1 means the fraction is upside down.

prompts.prompt: The normal question ends with a 2-mark 'given that' part. What are the two marks for?
prompts.answer: The first for the fraction, part (ii)'s tail over part (i)'s; the second for its value to 4 decimal places.

prompts.prompt: For n binomial trials, how do you find P(X ≥ 1)?
prompts.answer: 1 minus P(0), which is 1 minus q to the power n.

prompts.prompt: Given at least one success, what goes on top for 'exactly r successes'?
prompts.answer: The single term P(X = r) from the expansion; the bottom is 1 minus P(0).

prompts.prompt: A condition says a battery 'does not last more than 30 hours'. Which region is it?
prompts.answer: The left tail, T < 30: turn the words into an inequality before any arithmetic.

prompts.prompt: Both events say 'more than'. Which tail goes on top?
prompts.answer: The far tail, beyond the larger value: it lies inside the near tail, which goes on the bottom.

prompts.prompt: In a chain from the normal into the binomial, what becomes p?
prompts.answer: The normal tail for one trial, read from the table: the chance that a single item meets the condition.

prompts.prompt: Where does this specification stop for conditionals through a distribution?
prompts.answer: Every one is nested; a pair needing the area between two values, or a value found from a probability, is not set.

findings.asked: Less than 34 given less than 60, from two normal tails.
findings.wentWrong: Most multiplied the two probabilities on the top, not seeing that under 34 lies inside under 60.
findings.rule: If one event lies inside the other, its probability alone goes on top: divide, never multiply.

findings.asked: Less than 36 given less than 50, from two normal tails.
findings.wentWrong: Only the top 40% scored; the product on the top gave back 0.1151, the smaller tail.
findings.rule: An answer equal to the smaller tail means the condition changed nothing: divide by the condition's tail.

findings.asked: Three beads the same colour, given the first two the same.
findings.wentWrong: Under a third scored; most did not see that three the same already includes two the same.
findings.rule: Nested on a tree: the smaller event's branch total alone goes on top.

findings.asked: A conditional from a three-set Venn diagram, given not in one set.
findings.wentWrong: The numerator was usually right; the denominator was not.
findings.rule: The bottom is the condition's own group, counted first.

findings.asked: The first set won, given the second set won, from a tree.
findings.wentWrong: Many found the top or the bottom; only the best combined them.
findings.rule: Find both pieces, then divide one by the other.

insight.ruleToRemember: Sketch both regions; if one lies inside the other, the smaller probability alone goes on top. Divide, never multiply, and check the answer is below 1.
insight.aStarSignal: The full-mark answers wrote the fraction before any value: the smaller event's probability over the condition's.
